I want to be purely objective and transparent. The game itself is extremely fun, the graphics and combat are smooth and super engaging. This game has an extremely good potential to succeed. BUT and this is with an extremely disappointed heart, the game itself is 99% bots (excluding the very highest rank lobby which is 30 min to 1 hour que times). You will NEVER get a regular OR ranked match with a real player, if you enjoy this type of solo game experience with no meaningful interactions or realistic diverse player PVP then this will be a great game for you. However, a word of warning on this. If you intend to do ranked to earn rewards, BE WARNED the bot system they use will scale how tough/difficult they become. This does not sound too terrible on paper, but eventually the bots will have 100% perfect blocks/parries, 100% targeted focus on you the player, 100% perfect accuracy on your head, and extremely unrealistic dodging/avoidance and so once you reach a certain rank the system will make the game extremely unplayable and unenjoyable so please keep this in mind before attempting.

me too joined on beta.. well a lot less from beta came into reality on release, bots were since beta in games.. Seasung never removed em. they were a problem in all modes...
Verge First. so people literally had to grind to at least masters/GMs to meet other players.. like it was not hard, coz bots are bots.. but after reaching it vs easy bots- freshly baked players were met with reality checks.. meeting actual players that were destroying them and bots that literally have aimbot, wall hacks, and 10 times the energy than regular players.. and coz of terrible rank system- these new players could not derank, and pretty sure still can't (I left right as season 0 was ending, coz I saw nothing changing), and these players were just ruining games for others by existing there in high ranks.. but it was not even their fault.
Operation Storm/Mashmak- the extraction mode... tbh it was the best mode coz of unpredictability of what will happen, where and when enemy can appear, thrill of the hunt, and being hunted, ability to use a wide arsenal of weapons, true late game expirience of grinding and getting rewarded every run, even if u were not good, and for those who wanted more challange, and show every1 they can do it without full team of people.. those who knew how to play it- were bringing like 3-4 sets of weapons for different situations, radars, bunch of ammo for modular weapons, and whatever else, allowing you extract last even solo if ur teammates were executed, by pure skill and creative use of weapons that were bringing whole new layers and new oportunities for mechs that are usually locked in verge by base kit of the mechs.. it was fun af but... bots yet again.. and for some reason Seasung decided to split Mashmak we had in beta - 2 modes only (solo and trios), into... you will never guess.. 6... modes... 3 difficulties- normal (easy), hard (below average), extreme (just regular) for both solos and trios... deviding the player base for some reason, making it harder and even more not accessable for new players, coz everything below extreme was dropping literally nothing but paints.. no loot boxes, no good weapons, no good glider parts, no good mods, nothing. And then they also decided to scare new players away from it- by making it so, by dying, or being executed by a player- u will lose random mods u got, no matter the rarity. And mods were dropping with randoms stats.. so getting perfect mods was already not easy, but losing them- scared away a lot of players. And coz of small minority of players that were really vocal about adding PvE mashmak without any pvp.. well we got it, adding another layer of deviding the player base, and just removing any need in PvP mode... coz every1 could just guarantee the loot (losing to PvE there was pretty much impossible already in PvP extreme mode anyhow)..and where did it take us?.. Instead of having 2 modes for solos and trios, maybe 3 modes if adding 1 pve (unessasary at all).. we got 9 from what i saw with adding pve..
Ace arena- just unbalanced.. could be fun, but dnno.. meh.. should've not added it pretty much tbh, was least played mode anyhow.
.. Trading system- the lock of minimal prrice of irl currency to sell to other players.. bruh. why. But tbh for those who played extreme mashmak a lot corrite was never a problem... but for Verge players- it was impossible to get any cosmetics pretty much.
Shops.. well.. u guessed it corrite and irl money too.. and removed a lot of customisation options too.. and all customisation we had in beta was turned into presets- like lipstick, or eyes, or whatever- only in pre-set color.. can't change it.. even if u love how it looks but wanted another color- well bad luck, log in every week and pray u get the one you want, in perfect shade (there won't be any), from 2-3 per week, and ones u had last week can repeat next one.. good luck haHA.
So yeah.. ah also balance changes- some of em were just pulled out of no where, sometimes just traight up killing some mechs, making them nearly unplayable, or so OP it wasn't even funny.
people from ALL OVER THE WORLD in discord, here, on official site, in support even- all were telling them whats wrong with the game and how to fix it, every1 knew the problems... but they never listened... 
so yeah. Game had huge potential, it felt great to play, designs were pretty much perfect, etc.. but devs sold it all to make as much money as they can, and never listened to feedback, aside from dumb pve mashmak option, not even story mode, but mode to kill even more player interaction, making at a larp "pvp" single player game with nothing behind it.. not even a story like AC had.. and ended up just killing the game.

Disappointment of the decade for me. I enjoyed the beta of this game so much, and had incredibly high hopes for the full release. I was counting down the days to release, but when it came out all the magic died. Mecha games are just cursed to fail, it seems.

I finally uninstalled today.

The betas were better. For SO long, the balance was pretty all over the place over the games life span. The bots really do kill a lot of the fun because they're always present with no way to avoid them. You have to grind your ass off to get to player matches only EVERY season, and the casual mode rarely has any players. The Extraction shooter mode was an honest to god mistake to add or focus on and took away time and resources that could've been better allocated elsewhere. The 3v3 mode should've just been a custom room option. And for whatever reason they nerfed character creation from the betas into launch which probably put off all the dress up people since they could no longer make THEIR character their own. In the betas you used to be able to pick custom colors for so much stuff, such as a key one being eye color. In the launch and to this day they changed it to only preset color options.

The microtransactions were more like macro ones, we now have a gacha system for skins on top of that, they introduced a whole new paid currency just for that new gacha system, and finally the bots were never addressed once despite being brought up as a massive pain point before the game even launched during the betas.

I hope this game at least gets a private server like Gundam Evolution did, because I don't think this game really has much time left in it before its canned by the developers, who are clearly trying to extract as much money as they can from the few dedicated players remaining before they inevitably shut it down. Which I hate to say because its a REALLY solid game despite balance being all over the place. No other mech game really gave me the same feeling as playing Falcon and zipping around in the air barely avoiding death and often getting away with so much while holding on by a shred of health. I'll miss this game, but the developers kind of brought it on themselves.

During the playtests this game was incredible. It had fast, fluid mech combat where the better pilot actually won the match. The devs promised over and over that 6v6 arena PvP would stay completely fair, normalized, and skill based.
Well that did not last at all.

They dropped the Targeted Supply gacha banner with Custom MOD Strikers like the Falcon Cloudpiercer, and it completely ruined competitive mode. These are not just skins. They literally change your stats with armor piercing, faster lock-on, and insane boost regen. Calling it a sidegrade just because it lowers your base HP is pure nonsense, because anyone who actually plays competitive shooters knows burst damage and high mobility always win matches.
Worst of all, you can bring these straight into regular 6v6 and 3v3 ranked modes. To even unlock the full kit, you have to gamble through a six part RNG gacha banner with keys and real money.
I did not download an arena shooter just to watch it turn into a predatory mobile cash grab. If you want an actual competitive game where your wallet does not buy you combat builds, look elsewhere.

Uninstalling right now. Until they remove mods from PvP entirely, do not bother wasting your time.

As a high-quality free game, I want to recommend it, but not without major caveats. Unfortunately, the developers have made some frustrating design choices:

-Inventory Clutter: Storage space is limited, and cosmetic items count directly toward that cap.

-Paint & Pattern System: There are dozens of colors and patterns, yet every single mecha requires a separate unlock for each paint or pattern.

-Marketplace Restrictions: Player-to-player sales of acquired cosmetics are restricted to real-life currency (corite) with unreasonable minimum price floors.

-Exorbitant Pricing: Premium striker and pilot skins cost around $50, dropping only to $30 during discounts.

If you're looking to grind the ranked VERGE queue, be advised that the low active player count means high-rank wait times stretch to 5–10 minutes.

If these top issues were resolved, I would gladly give it a thumbs-up. But in its current state, I can't recommend it wholeheartedly.

# Mecha BREAK: A Competitive Game That Somehow Forgot to Build a Competitive Scene

Mecha BREAK is a spectacular-looking game wrapped around one of the most poorly thought-out competitive ecosystems I have seen in a PvP game. The actual mech combat can be fun, but almost everything surrounding it feels like the developers had absolutely no idea what kind of competitive game they were trying to build.

Amazing Seasun had plenty of experience with online games, but they had never established themselves as developers of a serious arena-based PvP game. Yet Mecha BREAK came out swinging with ranked systems, competitive aspirations, and even the apparent ambition of building an esports scene almost immediately. And it failed hard.

Instead of spending years building a healthy competitive ecosystem, establishing matchmaking, understanding player behavior, refining ranked progression, and then seeing whether an esports scene naturally develops, the game seemed determined to shove competitive gaming down everyone's throat from day one. The result is a competitive scene that is difficult to take seriously.

## Ranked Matches With Bots

Having bots in a PvP game is already questionable. Having bots in ranked matches is absurd. Having bots in ranked matches while simultaneously trying to present the game as a serious competitive title is next-level stupidity.

Then there is the complete lack of meaningful rank decay at the top. Watching a supposedly competitive leaderboard where players can sit in the Top 100 without meaningful rank decay is one of the dumbest competitive systems I have ever seen. A leaderboard is supposed to represent who is actively competing and performing well, instead Mecha BREAK can turn it into a museum exhibit. And somehow this gets even worse.

## The Blocklist Problem

The fact that players can influence matchmaking through their blocklists is genuinely baffling. If your matchmaking system allows competitive players to manipulate who they are matched against by strategically blocking people, then your competitive integrity is already hanging by a thread.

This becomes catastrophic in smaller regions. EU is the perfect example. When the active high-level population becomes small enough that the same players repeatedly encounter each other, top players can share blocklists and effectively manipulate the matchmaking pool. At that point, what exactly are we measuring? Mechanical skill? Team coordination? Who can manipulate the matchmaking system most effectively? Who has the right people blocked? Who can avoid the players they don't want to fight?

Congratulations, you have accidentally turned ranked matchmaking into social engineering. This makes statements from Kris, who apparently believes he knows what gamers want better than the gamers themselves, increasingly difficult to take seriously. If this is the direction the competitive design is heading, perhaps making mobile games would have been the more appropriate career path, because whatever Mecha BREAK is trying to accomplish competitively clearly isn't working.

## The "Competitive Scene" Is a Joke

The smaller the region, the worse this becomes. When you have fewer than 100 genuinely active players in a competitive region and those players can influence matchmaking through blocklists, the entire ranking system becomes questionable. You cannot build a legitimate competitive environment out of a population that small while simultaneously allowing players to manipulate the matchmaking pool.

Yet apparently this is supposed to become an esports game. An esports game needs a stable player population, strong matchmaking, transparent competitive rules, meaningful ranking systems, serious anti-abuse mechanisms, and a healthy ecosystem. Mecha BREAK has managed to make several of those things optional. But don't worry, at least we have another overpriced cosmetic bundle.

## Progression and Currency Systems

The progression system is another mess. There are too many currencies, too many systems, and too many layers between the player and the actual content they want. Instead of making progression feel rewarding, it often feels like the game is constantly trying to figure out which currency it can put between you and the thing you actually want.

The player should be thinking: **"What do I want to unlock?"** Instead, Mecha BREAK frequently makes you think: **"Which ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ currency do I need for this?"** That is not satisfying progression. That is an accounting department disguised as a game.

## Communication From the Developers

The communication doesn't exactly inspire confidence either. Competitive games require developers who understand that their community needs clear explanations, especially when it comes to matchmaking, ranking, progression, seasonal systems, and competitive integrity.

Instead, players are frequently left trying to figure out what the developers actually intend. When developers appear convinced that they understand what players want better than the players themselves, the disconnect becomes even more obvious. A developer can disagree with its community, that's fine, but if the community repeatedly tells you that something is broken and your response is essentially "you don't know what you want," eventually you have to consider the possibility that the problem isn't the customers.

## Too Many Modes, Not Enough Players

This might be the most obvious mathematical problem in the entire game. You have multiple game modes, ranked, different team sizes, extraction, different regions, and then a shrinking player population. What could possibly go wrong? Everything.

Instead of concentrating the remaining players into a healthy matchmaking pool, Mecha BREAK spreads them across multiple queues and then apparently has to use bots to fill the holes. This creates a death spiral: **fewer players → longer queues → bots → worse matches → players leave → fewer players.** And then the solution apparently is another game mode. Fantastic.

## The Biggest Problem

The biggest problem with Mecha BREAK isn't that the game is terrible. That's actually what makes it frustrating. There is a genuinely fun mech game buried underneath all of this. The combat can be fantastic, the mechs look incredible, and the core concept is strong.

And yet the developers seem determined to surround that good foundation with questionable competitive design, bloated progression, excessive monetization, fragmented matchmaking, and a baffling approach to player feedback. The studio had never established itself as a serious arena PvP developer and nevertheless seemed eager to push Mecha BREAK toward esports immediately.

Instead of building the foundation first, they tried to build the trophy room. Now the foundation is cracking: bots in ranked, no meaningful top-rank decay, matchmaking that can be influenced through blocklists, tiny regional populations, players manipulating who they encounter, multiple queues splitting the remaining population, progression systems designed like a spreadsheet, overpriced cosmetics, oversexualized character monetization, repetitive content, poor communication, and balance problems.

Mecha BREAK didn't need to become an esports game on day one. It needed to become a good competitive game first. Instead, the developers tried to sell us the esports fantasy before proving they could build the ecosystem. The result is a competitive scene that increasingly feels less like professional PvP and more like a private lobby with a leaderboard attached.

"A beautiful titan of steel, thoroughly choked by the weeds of greed."
How tragic it is to witness an engine of such immense potential brought low by the petty architectures of modern commerce. Every time I dare to step inside the cockpit, expecting the roaring symphony of an iron giant, I am instead assaulted by a relentless barrage of pop-ups. In-game solicitations, desperate and vulgar, screaming for attention to sell who knows what. They refuse to simply let me play.
## The Gacha Rot
The entire foundation of this experience has been warped into the likeness of a low-effort gambling house.

* 
* The Irrelevant Vessel: Instead of a battle-hardened commander, I am forced to look at a hyper-skinny, fragile pilot who feels completely divorced from the heavy metal they operate.
* Nonsensical Design: The interface is a labyrinth of bloated, goofy features I will never have use for. It is a system built not for depth, but for distraction.
* 

## Confusion as a Commodity
The game treats information like a weapon to be used against the player.

* 
* Unexplained Mechanics: Vital features are left completely shrouded in mystery, unexplained and abandoned.
* The Pop-Up Tutorial: When the game does condescend to explain its systems, it does so through the most irritating pop-ups imaginable—breaking whatever fragile immersion remained.
* 

## A Soulless Spectacle
I am confident there is a certain breed of modern consumer that thrives on this endless cycle of blinking lights and micro-transactions. Yet, I cannot help but look at the undeniable effort, visual fidelity, and mechanical polish that went into the core of this game and marvel at how utterly soulless the final product feels. Anyone can construct a playground of flashy make-believe, but true artistic triumph is broken by these greedy, limiting boundaries.
